title: IoT · 04 · Bluetooth, BLE mesh and Zigbee
notes: All page references are PDF pages. Bluetooth Classic limits and older BLE frame sizes are scoped to the legacy mechanisms discussed in the relevant slides.

Clarifications: 625 us is the Classic slot length, not a maximum packet duration; 3- and 5-slot packets exist. BLE advertising is followed by a connection request from an initiator/central, not a connection request from the advertiser.

The blanket claim that BLE cannot carry continuous audio is obsolete; pages 60–66 describe LE Audio and isochronous streams. Bluetooth SIG confirmation: https://www.bluetooth.com/media/le-audio/le-audio-faqs/

Numerical clarifications: -3 dBm is approximately 0.5 mW, not 0.5 W. Five hops means five links and four intermediate nodes; processing delay depends on whether endpoints are counted. Energy examples explicitly state which active intervals are included.

Ideal throughput, occupancy, interference and battery-lifetime calculations omit effects such as contention, listening, sleep current and battery self-discharge unless stated. They are not practical lifetime predictions.

questions.prompt: Choose a suitable WPAN approach for periodic tiny sensor readings, local audio and a building-wide sensor mesh. Explain why data rate alone is not enough to choose.
questions.answer: BLE suits periodic low-duty-cycle readings; Bluetooth audio profiles suit local audio, including LE Audio where supported; Zigbee or Bluetooth mesh can connect distributed sensors. Energy budget, range/topology, latency and compatible profiles also determine the choice.
questions.explanation: A fast radio can still be unsuitable if maintaining connectivity consumes too much energy.

questions.prompt: Explain the Classic Bluetooth piconet and scatternet. Can two peripherals in one piconet directly exchange data without involving its central?
questions.answer: A Classic piconet has one central controlling communication with active peripherals, traditionally up to seven. Peripheral-to-peripheral traffic uses the central. A scatternet interconnects piconets through devices participating in more than one.
questions.explanation: The active-device limit belongs to the Classic model, not every BLE deployment.
key_points: No direct peripheral exchange in that model
Scatternet joins piconets through shared devices

questions.prompt: Separate the responsibilities of the Bluetooth controller and host. What is the purpose of HCI?
questions.answer: The controller handles radio, link timing and low-level packet/link operations. The host runs higher protocols and profiles, including L2CAP. HCI is the command, event and data interface between host and controller.
questions.explanation: The split lets higher-level software control a dedicated radio subsystem.

questions.prompt: Compare Classic synchronous and asynchronous traffic. What does L2CAP do for asynchronous traffic, and why should its role not be assumed for every synchronous audio path?
questions.answer: Synchronous traffic reserves regular opportunities for predictable real-time delivery; asynchronous traffic flexibly carries general data and can use retransmissions. L2CAP multiplexes higher protocols and segments/reassembles data; the Classic synchronous path described bypasses that adaptation layer.
questions.explanation: Transport requirements determine both scheduling and stack processing.

questions.prompt: Classic Bluetooth has 625 us slots. Explain the role of hopping and why a 5-slot packet can last longer than 625 us without contradicting the hopping design.
questions.answer: Hopping spreads transmissions across channels to reduce persistent interference. A multi-slot packet stays on its initial frequency for all occupied slots; a 5-slot packet occupies 3125 us before the hopping schedule resumes.
questions.explanation: The slot clock continues to define timing even when a packet spans several slots.

questions.prompt: Describe the purpose of discovery, establishing a piconet connection and polling. Why must a peripheral know its piconet's timing and hopping sequence?
questions.answer: Discovery finds nearby available devices; connection establishes roles and shared link parameters. The central polls peripherals and schedules responses. Shared timing and hop information ensure peers use the same channel at the right time.
questions.explanation: Discovery alone is not a synchronized data link.
key_points: Shared hopping and timing are essential

questions.prompt: Why should a nearby battery sensor avoid transmitting continuously at the highest available power? Explain the reliability trade-off in lowering power.
questions.answer: Excess power spends energy and increases interference unnecessarily. Reducing power while preserving adequate link margin can save energy; reducing it too far raises losses and retransmissions, possibly undoing the savings.
questions.explanation: Minimum transmit power is useful only when the link remains sufficiently reliable.

questions.prompt: How can EDR increase payload rate while keeping parts of a packet compatible with Basic Rate reception? Why are guard and synchronization fields introduced?
questions.answer: EDR keeps the access-code/header portion at the Basic Rate GFSK format, then sends the payload using faster DPSK modulation. Guard time and synchronization support switching and correctly receiving the differently modulated portion.
questions.explanation: Increasing rate need not require every field to use the new modulation.

questions.prompt: Why does BLE suit small periodic readings? Explain the contributions of advertising, short exchanges and spending time with the radio inactive.
questions.answer: BLE lets devices announce small amounts of information without maintaining a continuous active stream, use brief exchanges, and sleep between events. Reduced receiver-on and transmit time lowers average energy use.
questions.explanation: Average duty cycle matters at least as much as instantaneous radio data rate.
key_points: Low duty cycle reduces average energy

questions.prompt: Compare the channel organization of Classic Bluetooth and the legacy BLE scheme described in the slides. Why separate primary advertising from connected data traffic?
questions.answer: Classic uses 79 channels spaced 1 MHz apart; BLE uses 40 channels spaced 2 MHz apart, traditionally three primary advertising and 37 data channels. A small known advertising set supports discovery without scanning every data channel.
questions.explanation: The figures describe different organizations of the same broad 2.4 GHz spectrum.
key_points: Known discovery channels simplify finding devices

questions.prompt: Trace a BLE device from being discoverable to an established connection. Distinguish advertiser, scanner and initiator roles.
questions.answer: An advertiser emits advertisements. A scanner listens and may request additional advertising information. An initiator sends a connection request in response to a suitable advertisement; it becomes central and the advertiser becomes peripheral in the connection.
questions.explanation: Advertising attracts a connection request; it is not itself that connection request.
key_points: Scanner discovers or asks for more information
Initiator requests connection and roles follow

questions.prompt: Compare passive scanning, active scanning and device filtering. How can scanning policy affect battery use and discovery latency?
questions.answer: Passive scanning only listens; active scanning also sends scan requests to obtain more information. Filtering limits accepted peers or messages. Less listening and fewer exchanges save energy but can delay or limit discovery.
questions.explanation: Discovery work costs energy even if no application payload is delivered.

questions.prompt: A connected BLE sender receives feedback showing that its peer still expects the previous packet. What does that imply, and why do sequence/next-expected indicators matter?
questions.answer: The previous data packet was not successfully acknowledged as received, so the sender needs to retransmit it. Sequence and next-expected indicators distinguish new progress from repeats, supporting acknowledgement and duplicate detection.
questions.explanation: An adapted reasoning question; it does not assume the slides' diagram labels form a general multi-bit sequence space.

questions.prompt: Why should the Classic limit of seven active peripherals not be applied directly to a BLE central with many sensors?
questions.answer: The Classic piconet limit comes from its particular addressing and scheduling model. BLE creates separate central–peripheral connections with their own event timing; practical connection counts depend on controller, scheduling and application resources.
questions.explanation: Connections sharing a physical central do not inherit every Classic piconet limit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish Bluetooth mesh Relay, Proxy, Friend and Low Power features. Which feature lets a phone interact without implementing the full mesh stack?
questions.answer: Relay forwards mesh messages; Proxy bridges access through GATT for a compatible non-mesh client; Friend buffers messages for sleeping Low Power nodes; Low Power nodes periodically poll their Friend. Proxy is the phone-access feature.
questions.explanation: These are distinct optional node capabilities, not four mandatory separate devices.
key_points: Relay forwards and Proxy bridges GATT

questions.prompt: A room switch publishes to group Kitchen. How should a newly added bulb be configured so it responds without changing the switch? Explain the benefit of group addressing.
questions.answer: Provision the bulb and configure the appropriate subscription to Kitchen. The switch keeps publishing to that group; membership determines which bulbs act, decoupling the sender from individual receiver identities.
questions.explanation: Adding a receiver need not require reprogramming every publisher.

questions.prompt: Why does mesh provisioning need more than radio discovery? Name the purposes of capability exchange, public-key/authentication steps and protected provisioning data.
questions.answer: Discovery only finds an unprovisioned device. Capability exchange identifies supported procedures; key exchange and authentication establish a protected trusted enrollment; provisioning data supplies the credentials/configuration needed to participate in the mesh.
questions.explanation: Merely hearing a device does not authorize it to join the network.

questions.prompt: Explain the Receive Delay, Receive Window and Poll Timeout in a mesh friendship. During which intervals can an LPN sleep, and what happens if the poll deadline is missed?
questions.answer: After polling, the LPN can sleep during Receive Delay, then listen during Receive Window for its Friend's response. Poll Timeout limits the interval between required friendship exchanges; missing that limit can terminate the relationship.
questions.explanation: Coordinated timing lets the Friend buffer traffic while the LPN keeps its radio off.

questions.prompt: In the managed-flooding mesh model, why does not every receiving node relay every message? Explain the reliability/airtime trade-off of relaying and repeated transmissions.
questions.answer: Only nodes with the Relay feature act as forwarders. Redundant relays/repeats improve delivery opportunities and extend reach, but consume airtime and energy and can increase contention; forwarding must therefore be bounded and managed.
questions.explanation: Many paths can improve resilience without making unlimited retransmission desirable.

questions.prompt: Give one mechanism emphasized for each of Bluetooth 5.0/5.1, 5.2 and 5.3/5.4. Explain why a version number alone does not prove a product supports every feature.
questions.answer: The deck highlights faster/periodic advertising and larger transfers around 5.0/5.1; isochronous channels, EATT and power control in 5.2; efficiency improvements in 5.3 and encrypted advertising in 5.4. Product support depends on implemented features and profiles.
questions.explanation: The question tests mechanisms, not a guarantee attached to a marketing version label.
key_points: Later efficiency or advertising security and implementation caveat

questions.prompt: A claim says BLE is unsuitable for all continuous audio. Assess it using the later slides: what enable LE Audio and synchronized delivery?
questions.answer: That blanket claim is outdated. LE Audio uses LE isochronous channels, introduced with Core 5.2, together with appropriate audio specifications and codecs such as LC3 to deliver timed audio streams.
questions.explanation: This qualifies the earlier slide rather than treating historical BLE limitations as universal. Bluetooth SIG: https://www.bluetooth.com/media/le-audio/le-audio-faqs/

questions.prompt: Compare CIS/CIG with BIS/BIG. Which structure fits synchronized connected earbuds, and which fits one source broadcasting to many listeners?
questions.answer: CIS is a connected isochronous stream; a CIG groups related CISs for synchronization. BIS is a broadcast isochronous stream and BIG groups related BISs. Connected earbuds can use coordinated CISs; broadcast listeners receive BISs.
questions.explanation: A synchronization group relates time-bound streams; connected and broadcast delivery differ.

questions.prompt: What problems do EATT and LE Power Control address? Explain why concurrent protocol transactions and dynamic transmit power can help different aspects of performance.
questions.answer: EATT permits concurrent attribute transactions, reducing blocking between independent exchanges. LE Power Control adjusts transmit power to link needs, seeking adequate reliability without unnecessary energy use or interference.
questions.explanation: Concurrency improves how work overlaps; power control changes radio operating conditions.
key_points: Power adjusts to reliable link needs

questions.prompt: A Friend has a 1000-byte queue for five LPNs. Each receives four 20-byte messages per hour. With no messages removed and no overhead, when is capacity reached? What practical factors change the result?
questions.answer: Input is 5*4*20=400 bytes/hour, reaching capacity after 2.5 hours. Queue metadata or larger frames reduce it; polling that drains messages increases retention time. This is a continuous average-rate estimate.
questions.explanation: Buffer lifetime depends on both arrival and service rates, not just message frequency.

questions.prompt: For two hours of audio, compare 345 kbit/s with 160 kbit/s. Using decimal MB, calculate transmitted data and the percentage reduction. Does this alone establish battery savings?
questions.answer: At 345 kbit/s the total is 310.5 MB; at 160 kbit/s it is 144 MB, a reduction of about 53.6%. Battery savings also depend on codec computation, radio duty cycle and other active circuitry.
questions.explanation: Lower bitrate reduces data volume but is not a direct full-device energy measurement.
key_points: Energy depends on more than bits

questions.prompt: Which parts of Zigbee come from IEEE 802.15.4, and what does Zigbee add? Why is 802.15.4 compatibility alone insufficient for interoperable application behavior?
questions.answer: IEEE 802.15.4 supplies PHY and MAC. Zigbee adds network formation/routing/security and application-support/profile behavior. Sharing a radio/MAC does not guarantee the same network or application conventions.
questions.explanation: Interoperability must extend beyond the ability to exchange raw frames.
key_points: Shared lower layers do not guarantee application interoperability

questions.prompt: Explain the different responsibilities of an RFD end device, an FFD router and the PAN coordinator. Which role best fits a sleeping battery sensor?
questions.answer: An RFD has reduced resources and communicates through an FFD parent rather than routing. FFD routers forward traffic; the coordinator starts and manages the PAN. A sleeping battery sensor fits an end-device role.
questions.explanation: The slides associate roles with typical power supplies; role capability is the essential distinction.

questions.prompt: Compare star, cluster-tree and mesh Zigbee topologies. What changes about alternate paths and the effect of a router failure?
questions.answer: A star depends on its coordinator for communication. A tree uses hierarchical parent/child paths, typically with one tree path between nodes. A mesh can use multiple router paths, so an alternate route may exist after a failure.
questions.explanation: Mesh resilience depends on actual redundant connectivity, not the word mesh alone.
key_points: Mesh alternate paths if physically available

questions.prompt: Describe how a new Zigbee node joins through an existing FFD and how hierarchical short-address allocation relates to a cluster tree.
questions.answer: The device discovers a suitable network and requests association through an existing FFD. On acceptance it becomes a child and receives network configuration/short addressing. In the lecture's hierarchical scheme, address blocks are delegated down the tree.
questions.explanation: Association establishes membership; hierarchical allocation organizes addresses among descendants.

questions.prompt: Trace on-demand route discovery with RREQ and RREP, and explain RERR and TTL. Why can reactive routing save work during quiet periods?
questions.answer: A source broadcasts RREQ to discover a path; an appropriate reply RREP returns route information. RERR reports a broken route; TTL bounds request propagation. Routes are sought when needed rather than constantly maintaining every path.
questions.explanation: Discovery saves idle control traffic but adds latency when a needed route is absent.
key_points: RERR broken routes and TTL scope

questions.prompt: Why can 2.4 GHz Zigbee, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth interfere despite using different protocols? Compare channel planning with frequency hopping as mitigation.
questions.answer: Their occupied spectrum can overlap. Planning places Zigbee channels away from heavily occupied Wi-Fi spectrum; Bluetooth hopping spreads exposure among frequencies. Neither method guarantees interference-free operation.
questions.explanation: Protocol identity does not isolate radio energy in shared spectrum.

questions.prompt: The deck uses 250 kbit/s for 2.4 GHz Zigbee and estimates 3/79 Bluetooth channels may overlap one Zigbee signal. What does that 3/79 estimate mean, and why is it not automatically the packet loss rate?
questions.answer: Under uniform use of 79 channels it estimates the fraction of frequency choices that overlap, about 3.8%. A packet loss also requires relevant timing, power and receiver conditions, so spectral overlap alone is not a loss probability.
questions.explanation: A simplified channel-selection probability should not be mistaken for measured end-to-end reliability.
key_points: Time and received power also determine loss

questions.prompt: A path has five links and four intermediate routers. Each link has 0.5 ms propagation; each intermediate router and the destination adds 2 ms processing. Exclude source processing and serialization. Calculate latency and explain your node count.
questions.answer: There are five processing nodes: four routers plus destination. Processing is 10 ms and propagation 2.5 ms, totaling 12.5 ms. Five hops count links, not five intermediate routers.
questions.explanation: This explicitly corrects the ambiguous hop/node counting in the slide exercise.

questions.prompt: At 250 kbit/s send an 80-byte frame, wait 192 us, then receive a 15-byte ACK. Ignore other overhead. Find transaction time and useful data throughput with continuous serialized transactions.
questions.answer: Data takes 2.56 ms and ACK 0.48 ms; including the gap gives 3.232 ms. Useful throughput is 640/0.003232, about 198 kbit/s, or roughly 79.2% of raw rate.
questions.explanation: Only data bits count as useful throughput; ACK airtime and the gap still occupy the transaction.
key_points: Payload-only numerator includes control time in denominator

questions.prompt: Assume a device consumes a constant 100 mW during a 3.232 ms transaction and does 50 transactions/day. Calculate transaction and daily energy. Why is battery energy divided by this number an optimistic lifetime estimate?
questions.answer: Each transaction uses 0.1*0.003232=0.0003232 J; daily energy is 0.01616 J. A lifetime estimate using only this neglects idle/sleep current, sensing, computation, retries, self-discharge and changing battery capacity.
questions.explanation: The given constant power applies to the entire transaction; real transmit and receive powers can differ.
key_points: Other energy costs invalidate literal lifetime projection

questions.prompt: Thirty-two sensors each send once every 30 s; each complete transaction occupies 3.232 ms. Calculate ideal channel occupancy per minute. Why might an implementation still see contention with such low average occupancy?
questions.answer: There are 64 transactions/minute occupying 206.848 ms, or about 0.345% of a minute. If sensors synchronize their reports, instantaneous demand can still cause collisions and backoff despite low average load.
questions.explanation: Low average utilization does not eliminate short bursts of contention.
